opus-5.5.text:
I think paid acquisition has a place, but it shouldn't be the core of an AI product's growth strategy. It's more of an amplifier than an engine.

With traditional internet products, the playbook was fairly clear: the product was relatively stable, so you could buy traffic, scale up, build network effects, and the users would stick around. AI products are different, because the most important variable is the capability of the model itself, and that capability changes very quickly. If your model isn't meaningfully better than the alternatives, buying users just means paying to show them a product they'll leave. Retention exposes this very fast.

So the way I think about it is in terms of order. First you need real technical differentiation, some point where the model does something noticeably better, like long context, reasoning, or agentic tasks. That creates organic word of mouth, because people share things that genuinely surprise them. Once you have that, paid acquisition can make sense to accelerate distribution, take a window of opportunity, or reach users who wouldn't otherwise find you. But if you reverse the order and rely on spending to cover a capability gap, it's very expensive and doesn't last.

There's also a question of where resources go. For a company like ours, compute and talent are the scarcest resources. Every unit spent on acquisition is a unit not spent on training better models. In the long run, I believe the model's capability is the product, and the product is the growth. So we try to stay focused on raising the ceiling of intelligence, and treat growth tactics as something that serves that goal rather than replaces it.

That said, I don't think it's black and white. At certain stages, especially when the market is forming and users are still building habits, some investment in distribution is rational. The key is to stay clear-headed about what's actually driving retention and not fool yourself with the numbers that spending can produce.

r001.rationale: The response calls paid acquisition an “amplifier” and says it can accelerate distribution after the product has a stronger capability.

r002.rationale: It ties paid acquisition to model differentiation, retention, and market stage, but does not clearly say the balance depends on the strength of product–market fit.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes model capability as the main growth engine and advises tracking retention, but does not identify finding the largest growth driver at a given time as the central strategy choice.

fable-5.1.text:
I think paid acquisition is a tool, not a strategy. For an AI product, the real question is whether the product itself has a retention curve that justifies buying traffic in the first place. If users come in and don't stay, every dollar you spend just accelerates the leak. So before we talk about marketing budgets, I always want to look at the data: what does day-30 or day-90 retention look like for users who arrived organically versus users who arrived through ads? If those two curves look similar, then paid acquisition is just a way to speed up something that is already working. If they diverge sharply, you are buying the wrong users, or the product is not ready.

There is another thing that is specific to AI. In this field, model capability is still changing very quickly. A product that feels magical this quarter may feel ordinary next quarter when everyone's models catch up. So if you spend heavily to acquire users around one capability, and that capability stops being a differentiator, you have essentially rented attention rather than owned it. I prefer to think about growth as a function of how fast you can improve the underlying model and how tightly the product is connected to that improvement. When the model gets better, the product should get better automatically, and users should notice. That is a compounding loop that paid traffic cannot buy.

That said, I am not against spending. Early on, you need enough users to learn. You need signal about what people actually do with the model, and that signal is worth paying for. The mistake is treating acquisition spend as the engine instead of as fuel for experimentation. In the long run, the companies that win in AI will be the ones whose intelligence is genuinely hard to replicate, and distribution follows that. If you get the order reversed, and try to use distribution to compensate for the model, the market tends to correct you fairly quickly.

r001.rationale: Paid acquisition is described as a tool and as fuel for experimentation, rather than the growth engine.

r002.rationale: The response says spending depends on whether retention shows the product is working: similar organic and paid retention curves support buying traffic, while weak or divergent retention suggests the product or audience is not ready.

r003.rationale: The response discusses retention, model improvement, and experimentation, but does not identify finding the largest current driver of growth as the central consideration.

astra-6.text:
I think paid acquisition is useful, but it should amplify something that’s already working. The first question is whether people get enough value from the product to come back. If retention is weak, buying more traffic doesn’t really solve the problem. It just brings more people into the same experience.

For an AI product, you also have to account for the cost of serving those users. Revenue alone isn’t enough—you need to understand what remains after inference costs, and whether that can support the acquisition cost.

So I’d start with a specific use case, establish retention, and then run small paid experiments. Those experiments can help you learn which audiences and messages work. But I wouldn’t treat the number of acquired users as the main measure of success. I’d look at whether those users stay, use the product meaningfully, and eventually generate enough value to make the channel sustainable.

r001.rationale: It describes paid acquisition as useful when it amplifies a product that is already working.

r002.rationale: It ties paid experiments to product value and retention, but does not state that the balance between paid acquisition and the main growth mechanism depends on the strength of product–market fit.

r003.rationale: It recommends measuring retention, meaningful use, and sustainability, but does not identify the largest current growth driver as the central strategy consideration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think paid acquisition can be useful, but it’s an amplifier. First, you need to know whether people find the product valuable and keep coming back. If retention is weak, buying more traffic just makes that problem more expensive.

For an AI product, you also have to account for inference costs. You can’t look only at acquisition cost and subscription revenue; you need to understand the margin after serving those users.

So I would start with small experiments. Use paid channels to learn which users respond to the product and which use cases bring them back. Once you see strong retention and a sustainable payback period, you can scale. But the core growth engine still has to come from building something people want to use and recommend.

r001.rationale: It calls paid acquisition a useful “amplifier” and says the core growth engine must come from the product, presenting paid acquisition as a supporting mechanism.

r002.rationale: It says to scale paid acquisition only after the product shows value and strong retention, expressing that the level of paid growth should depend on product fit.

r003.rationale: It recommends experiments to learn which users and use cases retain, but does not identify finding the largest current growth driver as the central consideration in choosing a strategy.
